title: Chlorinated paraffins in food
summary: European Commission recommends that EU Member State authorities and the food industry should monitor the presence of …
update:
The European Commission recommends that European Union (EU) Member State authorities and the food industry should monitor chlorinated paraffins in food from 2026 to 2029.

The monitoring will cover six food categories: fish, dairy products, oils and fats, meat and eggs, processed foods, and baby food. Testing will first measure short- and medium-chain chlorinated paraffins. More detailed testing will be required if their levels exceed the thresholds set out in Table 1.

These thresholds are not legal limits, so food containing levels above them will not automatically be considered unsafe or removed from the market. The aim is to collect data to help the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) to assess the risks of chlorinated paraffins.
impacted_products: Fish, milk and dairy products, vegetable and animal oils and fats, other products of animal origin (e.g. meat, eggs), processed foods (whole meals), baby food
what_changing:
The European Commission has published a Recommendation to EU Member States and the food industry to monitor the presence of chlorinated paraffins in food during 2026–2029.

The monitoring covers six food categories: fish; milk and dairy products; vegetable and animal oils and fats; other products of animal origin (including meat and eggs); processed foods (whole meals); and baby food.

Monitoring will initially focus on the sum of short- and medium-chain chlorinated paraffins (C10–C17). Where the chlorinated paraffin content exceeds the thresholds set out in Table 1, detailed testing should be carried out to measure all chlorinated paraffins, including long-chain compounds (C18–C30).

These thresholds are not legal maximum levels. Food found to exceed these thresholds will not be considered non-compliant and will not be removed from the EU market. The aim is to gather data that will support EFSA’s risk assessment of chlorinated paraffins.
why: Chlorinated paraffins are chemical contaminants for which EFSA (2020) has identified significant data gaps, preventing a comprehensive assessment of dietary exposure and potential health risks.
timeline: EU Member States and the food industry should regularly submit monitoring data to EFSA (see the EFSA webpage Data collection: chemical monitoring ).
actions: Future EU regulatory action will be based on the information collected by EFSA. It is therefore in the interests of the food supply chain to ensure that EFSA has comprehensive data.
resources: EFSA (2020) Risk assessment of chlorinated paraffins in feed and food . EFSA Journal, 18(3): 5991.
